name: Extended law of sines
whenToUse: You know an angle and its opposite side and need another side, or you need the circumradius of a triangle.
example: A triangle has $A = 30^\circ$ and $a = 6$. Then $2R = \frac{6}{1/2} = 12$, so $R = 6$. If also $B = 45^\circ$, then $b = 12 \sin 45^\circ = 6\sqrt{2}$.
pitfall: Each side pairs with the angle OPPOSITE it. Given two sides and a non-included angle, there may be two different triangles.
derivation: Draw the diameter from $B$ through the center, meeting the circle at $D$. Angle $BDC$ equals $A$ (same arc), and triangle $BCD$ has a right angle at $C$, so $a = 2R \sin A$. If $A$ is obtuse, $D$ lies on the other arc and $\angle BDC = 180^\circ - A$, which has the same sine.
